activities.anchor: Each part has its own failure modes
activities.caption: walk the loop outward — four stages in order
activities.name: csLoopOrder

config.prompt: The anatomy of one loop, in the order a correction flows:
items: Signal conditioning and conversion — amplify, filter, digitise
The feedback law — turns error into action
config.why: The art is that the loop is only as good as its weakest stage — a sluggish sensor or a wasted span starves everything downstream.

activities.anchor: What matters for control is not the sensor's chemistry
activities.caption: pair each transducer with its principle
activities.name: csSensorMatch

config.prompt: Five transducers, five working principles — pair them:

pairs.right: two dissimilar metals — a Seebeck voltage, microvolts per degree
a glass membrane, about 59 mV per pH unit
proof mass on springs, capacitive readout

config.why: What decides loop performance is the specification as an instrument — accuracy versus precision, range and span, resolution, hysteresis, and above all response time.

activities.anchor: Raw sensor signals are millivolts buried in noise
activities.caption: fill the signal chain's jobs
activities.name: csChainCloze

config.text: Amplification scales the %%0%% signal with a set gain while rejecting common-mode noise — the difference between a 5 mV signal plus 2 V of mains pickup and disaster. %%1%% — time-stamped storage — turns the loop's life into process history: trends reviewed after an excursion often show the disturbance you failed to %%2%%.
config.hint: One word per job: how the amplifier reads the pair of wires, what keeps the history, and what the excursion reveals about your plant.

activities.caption: contacts in series, parallel, or normally-closed?
activities.name: csLadderBuckets

config.prompt: Boolean logic lives in contact wiring — file each rung element:

items.label: the relay contact wired alongside the momentary start button
the stop button that breaks the rung
a safety chain where any failure releases

config.why: Power rails left and right, contacts and coils between them, evaluated top to bottom every few milliseconds — and the hard-won rule: emergency stops are wired, not programmed.

statements.s: Fail-safe means the system is safe from failure.
statements.why: It means the system fails into a safe state — the distinction is audit-ready.

statements.s: A guard-open wire that releases the brake is fail-safe design.
statements.why: A broken wire lands the machine in the safe state — the wire breaking does the stopping.

statements.s: A spring that shuts the valve when air pressure is lost is software logic.
statements.why: It is physical — springs, gravity, normally-closed contacts are the honest answers, not software.

statements.s: Every fail-safe design must answer what happens when power, signal and operator all disappear at once.
statements.why: That is the audit question — and the honest answers are physical.

statements.s: Emergency stops are acceptable as PLC code if the program is reliable.
statements.why: The safety function must not depend on the software working — e-stops are wired, not programmed.

activities.anchor: easiest to see on an oven holding 200
activities.caption: pin where a P-only oven actually settles
activities.name: csSettlePlace

config.prompt: The oven targets 200 °C but its heater must run at 40% forever. With Kp = 2, where does a P-only loop settle?
config.why: 20/2 = 10 °C below target — the arithmetic behind the oven's standing shortfall.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — what the stored windup demands
activities.name: csWindupEstimate

config.prompt: The door stands open a minute at 50 °C of error: the integral banks 3,000 degree-seconds. With Ki = 0.2, what fraction of a heater's capacity is the integral term demanding?
config.why: 3,000 × 0.2 = 600% — of a heater that can only deliver 100%. It saturates flat-out.
config.context: The humblest loop shows the same trade in miniature: the on-off thermostat buys a quiet relay with a ±0.5 °C hysteresis band.

activities.caption: which response is the high-gain-through-lag loop?
activities.name: csGainTrace

config.prompt: Two loops answer the same setpoint step (target = 5). Which one is high gain through lag?
config.why: Gain speeds response and shrinks offset — but gain through lag turns correction into overshoot, overshoot into oscillation, oscillation into runaway. Gain and phase margins exist to compute the limit before commissioning.
